record.paper_title: Local and Global Methods in Data Mining: Basic Techniques and Open Problems
record.original_question: Develop and characterize the limits of data-mining methods that are provably privacy-preserving; in particular, determine where the boundaries of provably privacy-preserving data mining lie.

evidence.quote: Problem 19 Explore the boundaries of provably privacy-preserving data mining.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let a dataset be a finite multiset D of records drawn from a domain X, and let a data-mining task be specified by a function f that maps D to an output (such as a set of association rules, a classifier, or a clustering). A randomized mechanism M is said to be provably privacy-preserving with respect to a formal privacy definition P (for example, differential privacy with parameter epsilon, k-anonymity, or a cryptographic simulation-based notion) if one can mathematically prove that M satisfies P on every input dataset, while still producing useful approximations to f(D).

Develop a theory that characterizes the fundamental limits of provably privacy-preserving data mining. Specifically:

1. For natural classes of data-mining tasks f (e.g., frequent itemset mining, decision-tree learning, clustering, regression, association-rule discovery), determine the optimal trade-off between any chosen formal privacy parameter and the achievable accuracy (utility) of M as a function of the dataset size n and the complexity of the domain X.

2. Identify which data-mining tasks admit mechanisms M whose accuracy approaches that of the non-private optimum as n tends to infinity, and which tasks are provably impossible to perform under a given privacy definition (i.e., establish impossibility results delineating the boundary between feasible and infeasible privacy-preserving mining).

3. Provide a characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions on f, on the privacy definition P, and on auxiliary assumptions about the data distribution) under which a provably privacy-preserving mechanism for f exists with non-trivial utility.

The goal is a rigorous demarcation of the boundary between what can and cannot be achieved by provably privacy-preserving data-mining methods.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is a broad research direction rather than a single conjecture. Since its posing, substantial progress has been made (especially via differential privacy, introduced by Dwork et al. in 2006, and subsequent work on private learning, private query release, and lower bounds), but the full boundary of provably privacy-preserving data mining has not been completely characterized. New impossibility and feasibility results continue to appear, so the problem is best regarded as still open in its general form, with partial answers for specific tasks.

status_evidence.title: Differential Privacy (Dwork)
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces differential privacy as a formal framework for provably privacy-preserving data analysis.
status_evidence.claim: A formal privacy definition (differential privacy) has been developed and is widely used to obtain provable guarantees, but it provides partial rather than complete characterization of limits.

status_evidence.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of upper and lower bounds for private data analysis tasks.
status_evidence.claim: Many tight bounds are known for specific tasks, but a full characterization of the boundaries of provably privacy-preserving data mining remains an active research area.
